p: Ali Adil Shah II was the eighth sultan of Bijapur. He came to the throne on the death of Mohammed Adil Shah on 4 November 1656, through the efforts of the prime minister Khan Muhammad and of the queen Badi Sahiba, a sister of the Qutb Shah of Golkonda. The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, who wished to annex Bijapur, found a pretext in doubts about Ali's parentage and, at the plea of his son Aurangzeb, sanctioned an invasion, although Bijapur was an independent ally of the Mughals and not their vassal. Aurangzeb had to raise the siege and hurry north for the war of succession to the Mughal throne.

With the accession of a young ruler, disorder began in the Karnataka, where the Nayaks tried to recover their former lands; Bangalore was Bijapur's administrative headquarters for controlling these feudatories. At court the struggle of factions for supremacy reached its height, and Aurangzeb intrigued with the Bijapur nobles and won over most of them. Shivaji meanwhile took more and more Bijapur territory, and his diplomacy prevented any coalition of the Mughals and Bijapur against him.

Through the sixteen years of his reign Ali fought both the Mughals and the Marathas, and he three times repulsed Mughal invasions. The reign was also marked by developments in Persian and Deccani literature and the fine arts. Beside the poet laureate Nusrati, the historian Nurullah wrote under his patronage a history known as the Tarikh-i Ali Adil Shah.

Ali died on 24 November 1672. By then the kingdom had lost most of its important territories, shrinking as Shivaji's kingdom grew, and the reign is seen as marking the decline of Bijapur. He was buried in Ali Ka Rouza, the monument at Bijapur known as the Bara Kaman.

notes: Short article (about 330 words of substance); 'Death and legacy' is under 60 words because the article gives no more.
The article judges the Mughal invasion 'wholly unrighteous' in its own voice; I kept only the fact that Bijapur was an independent ally.
The historian's full name in the article is Nūrullāh ibn Qāḍī Sayyid ʿAlī Muḥammad al-Ḥusaynī al-Qadirī.
Afzal Khan and Jai Singh, named in the entry, are not in the article.
